title: Excel Sheet Column Title
description:
# Excel Sheet Column Title

Given an integer `columnNumber`, return its corresponding column title as it appears in an Excel sheet.

Column titles proceed as `A, B, ..., Z, AA, AB, ..., AZ, BA, ...`, with column numbers starting at `1`.

For example:

```
A -> 1
B -> 2
C -> 3
...
Z -> 26
AA -> 27
AB -> 28
...
```

## Example 1:

**Input:** columnNumber = 1
**Output:** "A"

## Example 2:

**Input:** columnNumber = 28
**Output:** "AB"

## Example 3:

**Input:** columnNumber = 701
**Output:** "ZY"

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= columnNumber <= 2^31 - 1`

solutions.name: Reverse Append One-Offset Base 26
solutions.description:
## Approach

Repeatedly subtract 1 from `columnNumber`, take the remainder modulo 26 as the next character, and divide by 26. The characters are produced from right to left, so append them to a `StringBuilder` and reverse at the end.

## Key Insight

Excel column titles have no zero digit. Subtracting 1 before `% 26` shifts `A..Z` onto remainders `0..25`, which makes multiples of 26 correctly produce `Z` instead of an empty carry digit.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n), because each loop removes one base-26 digit.
- Space Complexity: O(log n), for the output builder.

solutions.name: Recursive Prefix Conversion
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same one-offset conversion recursively. After subtracting 1, the quotient is the prefix title and the remainder is the current last character. The base case is `columnNumber == 0`, which contributes an empty prefix.

## Key Insight

This mirrors positional notation directly: higher-order digits come from the quotient and the current digit comes from the remainder. The one-offset adjustment must happen before both operations.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n), because each recursive call divides by 26.
- Space Complexity: O(log n), for the recursion stack and returned title.

solutions.name: Stack of Generated Letters
solutions.description:
## Approach

Generate letters from low order to high order using the one-offset modulo rule, but push each generated letter onto a stack. Popping the stack produces the title from high order to low order.

## Key Insight

The conversion naturally discovers the last character first. A stack makes that reversal explicit and separates the digit extraction step from the final string assembly step.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n), because there is one push and one pop per title character.
- Space Complexity: O(log n), for the stack and result builder.

solutions.name: Fixed Back Buffer
solutions.description:
## Approach

Write generated characters into a fixed character buffer from the back toward the front. After the loop, construct the result string from the filled suffix of the buffer.

## Key Insight

The input is at most `2^31 - 1`, so the title has only a small number of letters. Filling from the back avoids both `StringBuilder.reverse()` and an explicit stack while still handling the one-offset digit rule.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n), one loop step per output character.
- Space Complexity: O(log n), because the buffer size is proportional to the maximum output length.

solutions.name: Exact-Length Back Fill
solutions.description:
## Approach

First run the one-offset division on a copy of the number to count how many letters are needed. Allocate an exact-size array, then run the conversion again and fill that array from right to left.

## Key Insight

This version shows that the title length is determined by the same carry process as the conversion itself. Once the length is known, each generated low-order letter can be placed directly at its final index.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log n), with two passes over the title digits.
- Space Complexity: O(log n), for the exact-size output array.

tests.description: The twenty-sixth column is Z, not a zero digit.
After Z, the representation rolls over to AA.
The second letter can advance after the first carry.
A two-letter title can end with Z.
The next value after AZ carries into the first letter.
First three-letter title checks the no-zero carry.
First four-letter title catches repeated carries.
Maximum int input checks repeated high-order carries.
